title: Euclid’s algorithm: what changes and what stays
goal: Trace the remainders, explain why the GCD is preserved and justify termination separately.

prerequisites.text: Nonnegative integers and the remainder operation.

sections.title: Why remainders make the problem smaller
paragraphs: We could try every possible divisor of 48 and 18, but division tells us that 48 = 2×18 + 12. Any common divisor of 48 and 18 must also divide 12.
Therefore gcd(48,18) equals gcd(18,12), then gcd(12,6), then gcd(6,0). The result is 6. Each transformation preserves the sought divisor.
Imagine two strips of length 48 and 18 cm. Cut both into identical pieces with nothing left over. Two pieces of length 18 leave 12, so now solve the same problem for 18 and 12.

sections.title: Pseudocode and state transitions
paragraphs: Start with (a,b). While b is not zero, compute r=a mod b, then replace a with b and b with r. The remainder is never computed with divisor zero.
For 48 and 18, the trace reads (48,18,12) → (18,12,6) → (12,6,0) → (6,0). The second component decreases after each iteration.
Every row uses the old b. Record the remainder before changing a.

diagram.caption: Loop pseudocode
diagram.text:
while b ≠ 0:
  r ← a mod b
  a ← b
  b ← r
print a

sections.title: Why the GCD invariant holds
paragraphs: If a number divides both a and b, it also divides a-qb and thus the remainder r. Conversely, a common divisor of b and r divides a=qb+r.
The two pairs have the same common divisors. Once b=0, the current a is the GCD for the stated valid input domain.
The invariant does not require a to stay 48. Both numbers change, but each pair has the same set of common divisors.

sections.title: Why the loop must stop
paragraphs: For nonnegative a and positive b, the remainder is nonnegative and strictly smaller than b. The second component cannot keep decreasing forever without reaching zero.
Inputs (0,18) and (18,0) both have GCD 18. In this teaching contract (0,0) is rejected explicitly because it has no unique greatest positive divisor.
Try the pair (18, 0). The loop condition is false before the first remainder, so the GCD is 18 and the number of replacements is zero.

sections.title: Build a safe C++ implementation
paragraphs: For strips of length 48 and 18 cm, find the longest equal pieces with no waste. The first division leaves 12 cm. What piece size will the replacements eventually yield?
Trace the loop on paper. Record the second value after each iteration.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and trace the steps
paragraphs: Read and validate inputs before the loop. We accept nonnegative values within int range, excluding (0,0). Production-grade code also needs bounds and input-failure handling.
To debug, compare the full trace, not only the last output. Calculate the remainder before overwriting the previous pair.
Trace the run with 48 18. If you assign a = b before b = a % b, the first remainder becomes 18 % 18 = 0. The program stops and incorrectly prints 18.

sections.title: Why the pair replacement preserves the GCD
paragraphs: If a = q·b + r, every common divisor of a and b divides r = a − q·b. Conversely, a common divisor of b and r divides a. Thus the common divisors are unchanged. With b>0, 0≤r<b, so the second value strictly decreases to zero. These arguments establish answer preservation and termination separately. For (18,48), the first remainder is 18; reversed inputs still work.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: The lab accepts integers a and b from 0 to 100000 except (0, 0). The worked C++ example uses the same bounds.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

sections.title: Try a separate task
paragraphs: For 84 and 30, find the GCD and the number of pair replacements. Print the two numbers separated by a space. Accept integers from 0 to 100000 except (0, 0). Print invalid for disallowed or unreadable input.
Predict the first case and one boundary case. Practice has a separate starter. After running it, explain which check or operation produced each result.

selfcheck.prompt: For input 18 48, trace the first replacement and then the remaining steps. What GCD does the program print?
feedback: Yes. The first replacement gives (48, 18), followed by the original trace.
18 is the first remainder, not the answer. The second value is still nonzero.
When b reaches zero, the program prints a.

selfcheck.feedback: Divisibility is preserved in both directions.

selfcheck.feedback: A nonnegative decreasing integer cannot decrease forever.

selfcheck.feedback: We exclude the two-zero case from this task's input domain.

practice.title: GCD and replacement count
practice.task: For 84 and 30, find the GCD and the number of pair replacements. Print the two numbers separated by a space. Accept integers from 0 to 100000 except (0, 0). Print invalid for disallowed or unreadable input.
criteria: Compute the remainder before replacing the pair and only when b ≠ 0.
Explain why the second number decreases and why 0 18 takes one replacement while 18 0 takes none.
practice.hint: Count only completed replacements. Compare 0 18 and 18 0.

steps.action: Add the loop and increment the counter after replacing the pair.
Check both the GCD and counter on boundary cases.

terms.definition: The greatest positive integer dividing both inputs without a remainder.
For nonnegative a and positive b, a%b is between 0 and b-1.
gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,a mod b), provided b>0.
A sequence of intermediate states such as a,b and remainder.
